CHR, a declarative language designed for logic programming with layered side effects, has multiple heads per atom in rule atoms, allowing local context capture from sibling subterms through argument indexing. This enables flexible local output and input interface management. We investigate the implications of CHR's design on its expressiveness compared to languages with static single-head logic programming, focusing on three key aspects: expressiveness augmentation, local output capture, and well-founded order among concurrent outputs, and demonstrate that these benefits come without sacrificing decidability in many common choice logic evaluations.

Galaxy rotation direction asymmetry has been a long-standing issue in astrophysics, 
with multiple studies suggesting it's real. We investigated this phenomenon using 
data from the Dark Energy Survey and compared its results to other sky surveys, 
including 2MASS, SDSS, Sloan-GALAXYS, ALFALFA, and 2MRS. We found the galaxy 
rotation direction asymmetry in the DES data to be similar to other sky surveys, 
but larger, and we attributed this to a more accurate method of aligning galaxy 
major axes. We also found that the DES data and others show a significant 
alignment of galaxy spins along a particular direction in space, 
$\ell = 253$,$\, b = -20$.

Meta-learning, a subset of learning to learn, has garnered significant attention in the field of machine learning. This research focuses on improving the robustness of the Riemannian Rank-1 update method, known as Eigen-reptile, which is a meta-learning optimization technique. Eigen-reptile was found to be less resistant to disturbances caused by the Riemannian projection used in its optimization process, particularly when the condition number of the Hessian matrix is high. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel meta-learning optimization framework, eigen-reptile with stochastic disturbance (ezen), to enhance the resilience of Eigen-reptile. Our analysis reveals that ezen maintains the same convergence rate as Eigen-reptile. Additionally, we extend ezen to handle noisy labels and demonstrate its superiority in several benchmark tests.

Automated analysis of medical images is a rapidly evolving field, yet remains a challenging task. In this research, we introduce a novel, easy-to-understand neural network framework, ICAM-reg, for classifying and predicting neurological conditions from MRI scans. ICAM-reg generates detailed, feature-specific explanations to identify patterns associated with various medical image characteristics. By applying ICAM-reg to data from multiple studies, we successfully employed it for identifying multiple sclerosis from brain scans and for segmenting various MS subtypes from lesion images. Notably, ICAM-reg consistently outperformed other neural network models, achieving high accuracy in the prediction of MS and segmentation of its subtypes. Our proposed method has the potential to significantly enhance the reliability of AI-driven diagnostic systems in the medical field.

The most significant challenge in AI morality lies in finding a way to measure the emotional impact of an AI system on its users, rather than simply assessing its overall morality. To address this issue, we propose a new approach to evaluating the emotional cost of an AI system by examining its behavior at the periphery of its decision-making model. Through this approach, we demonstrate the benefits of this method by applying it to the Fly AI moral measurement system and highlighting its advantages, which include reduced complexity and lower computational requirements compared to traditional evaluation methods.

We investigate the basic mathematical concepts underlying regular languages and their properties as subsets of infinite sequences or infinite strings.  Specifically, we focus on the "extent" of an automaton, defined as the set of all possible infinite strings accepted by an automaton.  We prove that for languages recognized by deterministic omega-automata, the extent is always a closed language, and show that for determinizable languages, the extent is always rational.  Furthermore, we show that for languages recognized by non-deterministic omega-automata, the extent is always a closed language, and proved that checking whether an automaton recognizes a rational language is decidable.

A cutting-edge cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) system has garnered significant interest for its ability to provide high spectral efficiency. The system's efficiency stems from utilizing all UEs for signal transmission and reception, thereby increasing the system's diversity gain. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of the system heavily relies on having a substantial number of antennas at the access point, a constraint that is difficult to implement in practice. The system's efficiency can also be compromised by the degradation of channels over time, a phenomenon that is addressed in this research. A novel approach, referred to as ACAD, has been proposed to optimize channel usage and minimize the impact of channel deterioration. The approach, an alternating scheme, involves training a deep neural network to assess channel quality and select the most suitable AP-AP subchannel pair while another network predicts the channel's remaining lifespan. The research demonstrates that ACAD outperforms traditional maximum ratio combining (MRC) method, achieving gains of up to 20% in spectral efficiency.

We utilize lattice quantum chromodynamics to investigate the impact of electromagnetic corrections on the axial-emission matrix elements of pseudoscalar mesons. Our findings indicate that these corrections align with a previously established framework, and we provide a numerical illustration of how these corrections influence the $V_{ud}$ quark mixing matrix element.

This research presents a novel neural network architecture for denoising residual images, called Identity Augmented Residual Dense U-Net (I-RDUN). I-RDUN combines the strengths of two prominent U-net variants, Identity Residual Network (IRN) and RDUN, to effectively remove noise from images and restore details. The proposed architecture features residual connections and attention mechanisms within each block, allowing for better information propagation and feature interaction. Additionally, I-RDUN incorporates identity components to enhance the network's understanding of clean images, thereby improving performance. Experimental results demonstrate that I-RDUN significantly outperforms other top-performing models in both subjective and objective evaluations, specifically in real-time denoising applications.

Multiview learning has garnered significant interest in the machine learning community, particularly in the context of neural networks. However, the theoretical underpinnings of this approach remain poorly understood. This study sets out to address this knowledge gap. From an identifiability standpoint, we establish that the loss function used in multiview learning can be broken down into two key components: a correlation term that captures latent multiview relationships and a self-guidance term that promotes consistent views. Experimentation reveals that the self-guidance term plays a pivotal role in the convergence of multiview learning. Furthermore, we show that the ability of an algorithm to converge is contingent on its capacity to identify and refine the latent multiview relationships underlying the data. These findings are expected to shed new light on the mechanisms driving multiview learning and provide insights into the design of effective multiview learning algorithms.

Galaxies exhibiting extreme redshifts in their mid-infrared spectra, particularly those with 3.6 and 4.5 micron readings significantly higher than those at 8.0 microns, are rare and require further analysis. These galaxies, known as HRIR galaxies, are found to have a higher mass of stars and a higher dust content than typical galaxies, indicating a distinct passive evolution. Our research suggests that HRIR galaxies are composed of an abundance of old stars and a substantial amount of dust, which is likely the result of a massive starburst event. These galactic structures are often found in the vicinity of massive, red elliptical galaxies, particularly in galaxy clusters, and are likely the result of a distinct formation process. Our data indicates that these galactic structures are not unique to clusters, but can also be found in smaller scale galaxy groups. Our research has also identified a correlation between HRIR galaxies and active galactic nuclei, suggesting a potential link between these galactic structures and the activity of a galaxy's central black hole.

In a study, we examined how humans and AI models handle moral dilemmas, specifically the well-known trolley problem. We provided participants with the classic scenario and alternative variations, asking for their decisions in relation to who should live and die. We then compared these results to those of two language models, GPT-2 and GPT-3, to understand their decision-making processes. Notably, GPT-3's predictions were surprisingly similar to those of humans, aligning in 70% of cases. Interestingly, humans and GPT-3 shared a common reasoning strategy when dealing with new or unusual trolley problem scenarios. These findings suggest that AI models like GPT-3 may be useful in testing and refining new scenarios for human moral evaluation.

A valuation domain $A$ is expressed as the limit of a sequence of complete intersection domains. This is achieved through a construction where each domain in the sequence can be generated by a limited number of variables over a finite field, satisfying a specific set of conditions. The complete intersection domains in the sequence can be identified by their unique Hilbert scheme associated to a certain collection of variables. The given construction extends earlier work by Gelfand and Macdonald, which applied to valuation domains of height 1.

This paper explores numerical methods for the two-dimensional Dirac equation under various conditions, including the Klein-Gordon equation, and examines how changes in boundary conditions, initial conditions, and parameter settings affect the results. The findings will serve as a basis for assessing the impact of different conditions on numerical simulations.

This study explores the effects of communication breakdowns on integrated systems combining Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control (CACC) and Platooning Adaptive Cruise Control (PACC). We've developed a hierarchical control framework using Linear Matrix Inequalities and Model Predictive Control, and we've identified the most critical communication pathways using a graph theory approach. We then formulated an indicator to signal communication breakdowns and derived conditions for their identification. These conditions are based on the state of the vehicles, the control inputs, and the communication topology. Moreover, we've identified the conditions necessary to prevent oscillations in string stability and maintain bounded string stability when the lead vehicle accelerates or brakes.

To evaluate the credibility of Twitter users, we developed an automated method that analyzes account behavior and associated news outlets. Our approach calculates an account's trustworthiness based on its interaction history with posted content and classifies users into reliable or unreliable categories. We then assess users by examining their posted content in terms of the information sources they follow and the users they follow, thereby estimating the reliability of the posted content. To gauge the effectiveness of our approach, we compare the posted content of reliable users with that of unreliable ones, thereby validating our earlier assessment of the users' reliability.

In V2X applications, providing low-latency communication is crucial, especially for urgent services. To address this need, we developed a new framework, called $\pi$-ROAD, that allows for real-time processing of urgent slices on demand. Unlike traditional approaches, $\pi$-ROAD leverages a dynamic learning mechanism to optimize communication slices in real-time based on the current network conditions. By combining machine learning algorithms with real-time network analysis, we can identify the most effective parameter settings for urgent communication slices. We applied this framework to a specific V2X scenario, where autonomous vehicles send emergency messages to other vehicles, and found that our approach significantly reduces processing latency compared to static configuration.

To address the issue of human and machine interaction in factories where AI-powered machines are increasingly prevalent, researchers have developed a novel wearable haptic interface for a collaborative system. The goal is to create a safer interaction experience between people and machines, and an experiment was designed to achieve this. The study involved having participants work together with a robot to accomplish a task, with the robot's behavior influenced by the operator's input, and an experiment was conducted to assess the impact of haptic feedback on task performance and safety ratings. The study's findings were based on self-reported safety ratings and performance metrics, and an analysis of these results provided valuable insights into the impact of haptic feedback on human and robot interaction in factories.

The rapidly evolving urban environment is reshaping how people interact with their surroundings, making it crucial to understand how cities evolve and adapt to change. Cities are complex systems that exist within a broader network of social, technological, and ecological relationships. As cities grow and develop, they undergo transformations that can be categorized into distinct patterns, with mobility playing a key role in these shifts. This research delves into the intricate relationships between cities and their inhabitants, examining the interplay of human and technological factors that influence urban development. To create a comprehensive model, this study draws on multiple perspectives and theories, including social network and complex system theories, to identify key patterns and processes in urban growth. The proposed framework, C-IF, offers a structured approach to studying cities and their dynamics. Using an empirical study of three cities, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of C-IF in uncovering underlying structures and processes in urban development, and its potential to inform the design of innovative mobility systems.

This paper explores the one-hop caching problem, where a user's preferences are predicted using a decision tree, and the caching system operates with an imperfect probability model of the user's choices. The objective is to minimize the expected number of items that need to be retrieved, knowing that each item can be placed in the cache with unlimited capacity and the user's preferences are revealed sequentially. A new strategy, based on a threshold zone, is introduced and shown to be effective in reducing the expected number of items to $\mathcal{O}\left(\log\left(T\log^2(M)/L\right)\right)$ for large $M$ and $T$, where $M$ is the number of items, $L$ is the leaf nodes in the decision tree, and $T$ is the time period. This strategy is optimal to within a $\log\log\log$ factor, and it is more efficient than a baseline scenario by a factor of $\log\log\log M$.

Automating the segmentation of medical images has become a pressing concern due to its extensive applications in clinical diagnostics. However, current deep learning-based methods are hindered by high computational requirements, which restricts their use for real-time analysis. To address this issue, we present a novel approach, the Trilateral Focus Network (TFN), which leverages a hierarchical architecture to concentrate on critical image regions while filtering out unnecessary information. By employing a trilateral loss function, our model can effectively reconstruct both missing pixels and high-frequency image details. Notably, our deep learning-based segmentation framework achieves a processing speed of 100 Hz on a mobile device, while its accuracy surpasses existing methods in various medical image datasets.

We have developed the off-shell harmonic $D=11$ superspace formalism for $\kappa$-Poincaré supersymmetry, focusing on the 4+7 superalgebra with 11-2-1 dimensionality constraints. This approach is based on a linearized superspace with 11-2 complex dimensions, where three bosonic dimensions are condensed into a single flat index. Eleven-dimensional Lorentz spinors are expressed as dual seven-dimensional forms with specific properties, and the superspace contains a single set of zero-symmetrized two-dimensional forms representing supersymmetry parameters. By incorporating a suitable zero-symmetrization, we can derive the eleven-dimensional spinor from seven-dimensional forms, and the superspace contains a single basis of zero-symmetrized two-dimensional forms, enabling the introduction of a suitable dualization for supersymmetry parameter functions. This approach allows for the introduction of a complexified superspace with one more complex dimension, facilitating the introduction of appropriate dualizations for supersymmetry parameter functions and the derivation of the $D=11$ supersymmetric $k$-form actions with $\kappa$-Poincaré supersymmetry invariance.

Machine learning models are often based on the gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) framework, which has proven to be an effective solution for a wide range of tasks. Despite their capabilities, GBDT models can falter when dealing with poor-quality data, which is a common occurrence in real-world applications. To address this issue, this paper presents an innovative approach to identify and mitigate the negative effects of data corruption on GBDT models. By analyzing the training dynamics of GBDT, the proposed method is able to detect anomalies in the loss function, which can be used to pinpoint instances that are out of order and potentially corrupt. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in accurately identifying corrupt instances, and a further analysis reveals that the proposed method outperforms traditional data validation approaches in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

In the context of quantum Hall effect, we explore the transformation of qubits. A qubit can be effectively formed using two states from the set of possible subband levels in quantum Hall systems by applying an external magnetic field perpendicular to the Hall material and restricting particle movement to these predetermined states. We investigate qubit transformations in both spin and pseudospin systems, discovering that anisotropic effective mass in materials exhibiting the quantum Hall effect facilitates a rotation in momentum space that is equivalent to spin rotation in regular qubits. A numerical model is employed to estimate the degree of accuracy for simulating qubit operations in materials displaying quantum Hall effects.

Recent advancements in autoencoding pretraining have led to the emergence of large-scale language models, which are capable of producing signals like text and images. However, the effectiveness of these models is hindered by the challenge of training them with their own generated signals, particularly when the training objectives are not aligned with the pretraining task. To address this limitation, a novel method called Model Produced Signal denoising, or MPS-denoising, has been proposed. This method involves training the autoencoder model by minimizing the evidence lower bound, or ELBO, using the latent code produced by a pretraining task, rather than the signal produced by the autoencoder model itself. To achieve this, a new training objective is derived by combining the ELBO and a signal classification loss, which is then optimized through a novel method called iterative path sampling. The results show that MPS-denoising significantly outperforms previous methods, including full denoising, in terms of both signal quality and model performance.

Inferring the structure of a complex quantum network from limited data is crucial to its secure operation. This study focuses on determining the connections within an anonymous network consisting of distinct 'nodes' of varying sizes. By analyzing individual feedback from each node, researchers aim to uncover the complex network architecture. Building upon previous research, this investigation relaxes certain constraints and explores the effectiveness of modified greedy algorithms in achieving this goal. A key contribution is the development of a quantum version of a classic statistical test used in classical network structure inference.

To better comprehend how people interpret and use visual representations, we conducted a study involving crowdsourced descriptions of 57 introductory-level data visualizations. The descriptions provided by the participants were analyzed and categorized to identify the types of insights they offered, which included identifying patterns, controlling for bias, making comparisons, and drawing inferences. The results showed that most descriptions focused on pattern recognition, followed by comparative analysis, then inferring relationships, and a few instances of controlling for bias. Additionally, we compared these crowdsourced descriptions with existing literature and found that they more frequently conveyed insight into pattern recognition and comparative analysis, whereas literature tended to convey insight into identifying patterns, controlling for bias, and inferring relationships. The findings of this study have implications for the design of data visualizations aimed at educating beginners.

Lieb's theorem establishes that at absolute zero, a peak entropy occurs in Bose-Einstein condensation when the ratio of particle number to interaction strength approaches infinity.  In this limit, the ground state energy scales cubically with particle number, not quadratically as in the case of a single isolated particle.  The peak entropy occurs because the scaling of the ground state energy dominates the total energy, making the thermodynamic limit irrelevant.  This note reviews peak entropy BEC, focusing on the theoretical framework and highlights the scaling of the third virial coefficient in establishing the third-law-of-mathematical thermodynamics.  Theoretical models of peak entropy, including the attractive delta-function potential, have been developed and studied, and research continues to investigate the properties of these systems.

Counterfactual explanations are being used in machine learning-based decision systems to increase transparency and trust. However, the current methods for generating these explanations are limited in addressing uncertainty in the models, particularly when dealing with multiple possible distributions. In real-world applications, the data distribution is often unknown, and the model output can change based on shifts in the distribution. In response to this challenge, we propose a new approach for creating counterfactual explanations under uncertain data conditions. Our method involves identifying the most uncertain areas in the decision boundary and using a novel optimization problem to develop strategies for dealing with distributional uncertainty. Our proposed algorithm offers a more efficient solution for explaining model outputs under uncertain conditions, as demonstrated in our experiments using real-world datasets.

Urban noise pollution's negative effects on residents' quality of life have prompted various initiatives to mitigate it. Evaluating noise pollution's impact and tracking the effectiveness of mitigation strategies require noise models that can be robust and adaptable. A novel dataset, NOISECAT, has been developed to support the noise pollution's classification and estimation tasks. This dataset features a comprehensive set of ground-truth labels, carefully curated urban noise samples, and an open-source codebase for seamless data integration. As a pioneering multi-class urban noise categorization dataset, NOISECAT bridges the gap between academic and industry research by providing a standardized framework for comparing noise classification algorithms. To foster a standardized approach to noise classification, a set of baseline models has been introduced, and the dataset is publicly available at https://noiseusc.github.io/NOISECAT/.

We focus on finding supersymmetric AdS4 black holes within specific gauged supergravity theories that combine massless tensor and complex vector fields with their respective matter counterparts. These theories, which are part of a broader classification strategy of gauged supergravity theories, yield novel AdS4 black hole solutions in N=3 and N=4 supersymmetry. Specifically, the N=3 theory provides two families of N=1 supersymmetric AdS4 black holes, while the N=4 theory yields three distinct families, including a new N=4 solution that is distinct from existing N=4 AdS4 black hole results.

A crucial component in computer vision is convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are a type of neural network that applies weight and bias information to generate feature maps from input data. Implementing CNNs on camera sensors allows real-time data processing without needing to transfer data to external processors. To create optimized code for CNNs, a new tool called Cain is proposed. Cain can automatically generate optimized code for CNNs on camera sensors using information from a CNN's weight matrix, hardware specifications, and programming language. When compared to hand-optimized code, Cain produces similar results, with code execution times being only 5-18% slower. Furthermore, when running on multiple cores, code generated by Cain can achieve speedups of up to 2.5 times faster than optimized code.

We examine the moduli space of type IIB string theory compactified on a six-dimensional orbifold, specifically with regards to their effective field theories. The moduli for complexified string parameters are identified as having global supersymmetry broken by a global term, and the moduli for parameters with a remaining supersymmetry are subject to breaking by a specific theta-term. The global term and theta-term are determined by the moduli's action on the parameters, and the parameters' contribution to the parameters' potential is identified. The parameters' extended theta-terms are then derived and the parameters' global supersymmetry-breaking terms are identified. The moduli space parameters' global supersymmetry-breaking terms are found to be related to the parameters' extended theta-terms.

A novel, simulation-driven approach to learning equilibrium in games is presented, which incorporates regret minimization techniques to strike a balance between the goals of minimizing losses and achieving optimal game outcomes. By combining these objectives, the method, known as remorse pruning, optimizes the trade-off between the effectiveness of the equilibrium and its associated losses, allowing for a more efficient use of game data. Through theoretical analysis and verification on multiple scenarios, the method has been shown to effectively address the challenges posed by high-dimensional games and achieve improved performance.

Aristotle's modal syllogisms have been a topic of discussion for centuries, with a recent paper presenting a formal system that can logically interpret them. This paper builds upon that framework, providing a formal semantics and proof-calculus for a modified version of the system, as well as demonstrating its validity through the derivation of several theorems, including those for syllogisms with transitive relationships, in a context with an unspecified world. Furthermore, we provide a natural deduction system and prove its soundness and completeness relative to our established semantics.

Quantum causation is an issue that arises when quantum systems are influenced by the measurement process, leading to potential causality issues. Quantum systems, in an attempt to avoid this problem, may exhibit unpredictable behavior. Researchers have proposed a new concept, detection vulnerability, which quantifies this problem in quantum systems. Detection vulnerability is found to be directly related to the degree of unpredictability in quantum correlations, and it can be utilized to identify and analyze the impact of various types of quantum correlations. A key finding is that certain types of entanglement and Bell correlations are more susceptible to detection than others. Furthermore, the study suggests that using specific error correction methods can reduce detection vulnerability, and proposes a new metric, detection ratio, which can be used to assess the effectiveness of these countermeasures.

This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning-based framework for dynamic bit and quality optimization in the HEVC video coding standard. The proposed approach employs the multi-frame network structure to simultaneously determine bit allocations for all frames within a coding unit's coding tree unit on the encoder's side. The optimization process involves allocating each coding unit's total allocated bits to its constituent blocks during the coding tree unit encoding stage. The framework's dual-critic network enables efficient joint optimization of quality and bit allocation by leveraging two separate critic networks: one for predicting long-term video quality and the other for predicting cost in the coding unit encoding process. The agents' training involves interacting with both networks. The proposed method is compared to the HEVC reference encoder in single and multi-pass configurations using various test scenarios. The results demonstrate that the top-performing RL-based framework achieves 4.29% and 4.51% improvements in PSNR over the multi-pass and single-pass HEVC encoders, respectively, under low-complexity conditions.

The formation of planets is preceded by a proto-planetary disk, which is a disk of dust and gas that forms around a young star after the star formation phase.  The chemical composition of this disk is a critical factor in the formation of planets and the development of their atmospheres.  In this study, we investigate the chemical processes that occur in the proto-planetary disk, specifically the interactions between dust and gas.  We have developed a new model that takes into account the thermal and chemical properties of the gas and the mass loss of dust particles, which is an important factor in the chemical evolution of the disk.  Our model is consistent with observations of the proto-planetary disk, specifically the abundance of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.  We have also found that the mass loss of dust in the proto-planetary disk is a critical factor in the chemical evolution of the disk, which is in agreement with previous studies.  In contrast to previous studies, we have found that the mass loss of dust in the proto-planetary disk is a critical factor in the chemical evolution of the disk, which is a critical factor in the formation of planets and the development of their atmospheres.  The chemical evolution of the proto-planetary disk is a complex process that is influenced by the mass loss of dust and the interactions between dust and gas.
