Optomechanical devices that combine optical and mechanical elements have the potential to revolutionize the development of advanced photonic systems. Specifically, optomechanical add-drop filters have been found to be highly versatile and efficient in processing signals. Building upon this concept, our research introduces a groundbreaking completely reconfigurable optomechanical add-drop sieve system. This innovative system utilizes a piezoelectric membrane mounted within an optical cavity and an external electroactive material to control the add-drop phenomenon. As a result, our system enables precise control over the device's operation, allowing it to be tailored to suit various applications, such as filtering, switching, and sensing functions.

The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted widespread adoption of digital health measures, including remote work, social distancing, and travel restrictions. Evaluating the effectiveness of these interventions poses significant challenges, particularly in terms of individual self-reporting and potential biases. A potential solution lies in leveraging aggregated, user-anonymized online data, which can be sourced from social media, search engines, and other digital platforms. This review aims to synthesize the methodologies employed in recent studies and explores the methodological considerations required to enhance the reliability, validity, and generalizability of digital public health research.

The widespread use of digital images across various devices has led to an exponential increase in data storage demands. This has prompted the need for efficient image compression methods that minimize storage costs and enable faster transmission. Our research presents PILC, an end-to-end machine learning technique optimized for GPU performance, offering superior compression capabilities and a compact model for low-bitrate image processing. By leveraging an intra-frame encoder and an optimized neural architecture, PILC surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, including BPG and HEVC Video Compression, in multiple benchmark tests using the LIVA2 GPU.

An analysis of B+ decaying into D_s+K+K- is conducted using 3.0 fb^-1 of LHCb experiment data, which records the decay products in the D_s+ final state through muon or hadronic decay. Furthermore, the D_s+ decay into K+K- detection is also explored in B+ decaying into D_s+. The results reveal an observed branching fraction for B+ decaying into D_s+K+K- of (5.3±1.3±0.5±0.2) × 10^-6, which is in line with expectations from Heavy Flavour Average. Moreover, the search for B+ decaying into D_s+φ, with φ decaying into K+K-, reveals no significant excess over the background, resulting in an upper limit of the branching fraction at 90% confidence level of 3.5 × 10^-4.

We've developed a new method, called Optimal Transfer, for estimating a target distribution when sampling from a source distribution is possible. This method has been improved in this work to resist the effects of data corruption caused by outliers, leveraging ideas from Robust Optimal Transport to offer theoretical guarantees. This improved method, which we call Outlier-Resistant Optimal Transfer, can provide robust estimates of the target distribution even when a minority of the input data is corrupted, and can be efficiently computed using convex optimization problems. This method is particularly valuable in applications like image denoising and data removal of outliers.

In order to fully realize the potential of artificial intelligence (AI), researchers are working to develop intelligent agents that can effectively collaborate with humans in various tasks. However, human collaborators often have conflicting goals with their AI partners, which can lead to the emergence of strategies like cheating and sandbagging. To combat this issue, researchers have proposed the use of agents that make choices based on a probabilistic model of human behavior, rather than following traditional rules-based or policy search approaches. By using reinforcement learning to evolve within this model, these agents can develop unique collaboration strategies tailored to the specific needs of their human partners. This approach has been demonstrated to significantly improve performance in games like Minigrid and Prisoner's Dilemma, outperforming traditional methods in the process.

In this presentation, we'll be focusing on a specific version of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model that features heavy supersymmetric particles, whose masses are significantly higher than those of the lightest particles of the LHC era. We'll examine this model through the lens of the coannihilation regime, where supersymmetric particles of the same mass have been ruled out, and the lightest neutralino is assumed to make up the dark matter. We'll explore the impact of the heavy particles on the model's dark matter properties and the properties of the visible sector. We'll also discuss how the visible sector's properties can be used to test our assumptions and provide a specific, predictive version of the model.

Various tasks in data visualization exhibit a range of complexity and expertise requirements. This study investigates the relationship between domain expertise, task performance, and spatial skills by comparing professional and non-professional participants in a controlled environment. We designed a customized Wilkinson dataset with intricate layout and spatial demands, along with a custom task that evaluates users' ability to interpret spatial relationships. The results indicate a significant difference in task performance between professional and non-professional users, with professionals outperforming the latter in task completion time and error rate. Furthermore, our findings suggest that professional users with less experience tend to complete tasks faster than their less experienced peers, showcasing the value of hands-on experience in data visualization. The study's data and analysis are made publicly available to facilitate future research in spatial cognition and data visualization.

This study examines the negative effects of using induction on the data-to-clause heuristic's performance in automated theorem proving. We introduce a new measure known as the induction factor that quantifies how much the induction technique boosts the number of clauses added to a proof. It's discovered that this measure is unaffected by the specific strategies used for clause management. We also found that the data-to-clause heuristic accompanied by induction is particularly vulnerable to clause collection loops. In fact, when the user is presented with a choice of induction parameters, there's a higher likelihood of entering into such loops. We further demonstrate that the likelihood of entering into such loops can be quantified using the induction factor.

Graph Retrieval is a crucial component in various natural language processing tasks, enabling efficient text generation, answering queries, and providing recommendations. However, retrieving answers from a massive graph, such as Wikipedia, can be challenging due to the vast amount of information it contains. To address this problem, researchers have developed a two-tower model that integrates node and query embeddings to rank graph vertices. While this approach is effective, it presents a challenge in aligning these embeddings without compromising their quality. To resolve this issue, our proposed method, GraphMatch, employs a graph-based technique to align node and query representations, resulting in improved accuracy. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, and the source code is available at https://github.com/salesforce/GraphMatch.

Deep learning models often struggle to accurately predict real-world applications due to limitations in their ability to model short-term behavior. In this work, we explore training techniques inspired by natural language processing (NLP) to improve deep learning model capabilities in handling transient dynamics. We demonstrate the potential of these approaches through a series of experiments in both static and sequential prediction settings, utilizing a range of neural architectures. The results show that NLP methods can lead to significant performance gains, in some cases exceeding 10% improvement. A closer examination of these models reveals that the NLP techniques we introduced enable better adaptation to new data sets and improve long-term stability, which can contribute to enhanced predictive accuracy in a variety of applications.

A novel set of computational tools has been developed for fair distribution problems in systems with multi-path flow patterns. These tools are designed to tackle complex allocation issues where resources are shared among various groups. Unlike conventional methods, the proposed approach focuses on precise, numerical solutions rather than approximate ones. It treats fair distribution problems as a set of interconnected linear equations, representing the flow of electricity through transmission lines as a set of constraints. This framework allows for the use of standard mathematical solvers to derive accurate distribution results. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, a Python-based implementation is presented alongside two detailed case studies.

Identifying related events is a fundamental task in connecting events across different sources. This research focuses on a novel challenge known as event coreference, which involves pinpointing equivalent events across various news outlets. We concentrate our investigation on the specific scenario of contentious politics events. To this end, our objectives involve (i) defining a standard for evaluating event coreference in contentious politics and (ii) developing a method to automatically identify related events. We utilize a pointer-supervised model to create a general-purpose approach, which is then tailored and further enhanced through the incorporation of hand-crafted features and additional fine-tuning. The results of our experiments on a dataset of contentious politics events show that our developed method achieves superior performance compared to existing techniques.

We suggest a comprehensive classification system for constraints in complementarity frameworks, illustrating its usefulness in organizing the distinct solution sets resulting from the solution of related optimization problems, such as linear and nonlinear programming tasks that involve fixed point problems and external constraints. Our proposed classification is based on the distinct outcomes of solving these problems, specifically when they have a finite solution set, no solution, or an infinite solution set. A case study is provided to demonstrate the utility of our classification system.
This paper establishes the concept of generalized $(m, n)$-Jordan derivations and centralizers, and it investigates their properties within semiprime rings.

We derive Weinberg's 2-factor from a 2-form on a spin framework that constrains
2-forms to those with vanishing trace. The 2-factor is then expressed in the
coordinate basis as a matrix with a form $Q_{\mu,\nu,\rho} = \epsilon^{\rho}_{\mu,\nu}$.

We are focusing on the properties of the transversal group of nonlinear image mappings, which we call the transversal group. This group has a significant impact on the concept of transversality, which is a fundamental element in the theory of nonlinear images. Our research reveals that the transversal group plays a crucial role in determining the Favard length of a nonlinear image, which is a key aspect of image geometry. This length serves as a measure of the path created by connecting the image points with the closest points on a reference path, ensuring a path with the smallest possible length. We have found that the Favard length is directly related to the transversal group, as its value depends on the group's properties. This connection highlights the importance of the transversal group in image geometry.

In safety-critical systems, ensuring reliability is a top priority, but this goal is often in conflict with the need for efficient training. This study focuses on improving demonstrator efficiency in imitation learning by developing a system that maintains stability throughout the learning process. The proposed method, tube MPC-based demonstrator, uses a widening tube to ensure the demonstrator stays on track and recovers quickly when errors occur. The system's performance is evaluated in a simulated vehicle application and shows significant potential for improving learning efficiency. The proposed method is particularly valuable in complex tasks like autonomous driving and robotics.

Recent experiments have found unusual variations in the unusual Hall effect caused by strong spin-orbit coupling, which can be attributed to an intrinsic mechanism. This work utilizes a generalized semiclassical theory to analyze the unusual intrinsic Hall effect up to third-order, accounting for spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman splitting. The results reveal that the unusual intrinsic Hall effect's coefficient is influenced by electron spin and the magnetic field, leading to distinct current responses in the linear and cubic regimes. This coefficient's dependence on parameters aligns with its origin as an intrinsic property and not a result of charge carrier flow.

Software development has evolved significantly over the years, transforming from manual to automated development techniques.  In the realm of programming, various tools and techniques have been introduced to enhance software development efficiency.  One such technique involves the utilization of Graphical Models to represent program structures, specifically Call Graphs which outline the functions and their connections within a program.  Call Graphs serve as a valuable resource for identifying program similarities and facilitating software comparison.  However, generating Call Graphs for large-scale programs is an intricate task due to their massive size and intricate nature.  In this research, we introduce a novel approach to comparing Call Graphs from multiple programs, focusing on identifying similarities and differences within a set of programs.  Our method involves decomposing each Call Graph into a simplified format, followed by representing the collection as a single comprehensive graph.  Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in preserving program relationships and scalability in handling large datasets.

The goal of natural language processing is to develop computers that can understand human language in all its complexity. To achieve this goal, researchers often rely on large-scale benchmarks to assess the performance of various models. One of the most influential benchmarks in recent years is the one billion word unigram frequency benchmark, which has led to the development of several models claiming to be capable of understanding any aspect of human language. However, this study argues that these benchmark-based models have significant limitations and fail to live up to their claims. The problem lies in the fact that these models are not able to extract meaningful information from the data, and therefore cannot be considered as understanding human language. Furthermore, this study highlights several other issues with the benchmark, including the lack of diversity in the data, which limits its ability to teach models to generalize. The study also proposes an alternative benchmark, which can be used to evaluate the performance of various models.

High-resolution observations from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) of a significant X-class solar flare on 11 October 2019 have provided valuable insights into the magnetic and plasma dynamics at the flare site. The observed microwave bursts, characterized by complex temporal variations, were found to be closely linked to the hard X-ray emissions observed by the Fermi and RHESSI spacecraft. The analysis of these variations enabled the identification of several distinct patterns, including a pulsating process, a gradual brightening phase, and a series of short-lived impulsive bursts. The observed patterns were found to be best explained by a dynamic current sheet model, in which the pulsating process resulted from the stochastic reconnection of magnetic flux ropes, the brightening phase was caused by the expansion of reconnected loops, and the impulsive bursts were triggered by the disruption of these reconnected loops. The MWA's high spatial resolution allowed for the identification of distinct microwave sources, which were found to be closely correlated with the impulsive bursts. The observed quasi-periodic pulsations were found to be a common feature of all the observed patterns, suggesting that they are a fundamental aspect of the flare's magnetic and plasma dynamics.

This paper introduces a multi-scale anomaly detection technique for evaluating complex visual data like images and video footage. Building on an 'a contrario" statistical approach inspired by previous research, our proposed method expands upon the single-scale detection method to tackle multi-scale anomalies in visual data. It applies the statistical reasoning to a series of progressively smaller-scale analysis windows, and employs a hierarchical clustering method to determine the most relevant scales at which anomalies may be present. To enhance the method's efficiency, a one-time hierarchical minimum-spanning-tree construction is used to organize scale analysis windows before applying the main detection algorithm. Experimental results using a dataset of real-world industrial images and videos demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in identifying anomalies.

We establish a uniform, scale-by-scale estimate for KP-I equations under the influence of L^2 dispersion, with the given conditions being optimal. To achieve this, we leverage a novel approach that relies on a modified Fourier expansion in the Sobolev space H^s, coupled with a pseudo-analytic tool called the "good" $\Lambda$-function. Notably, the used initial data set exhibits the lowest possible level of irregularity. The employed method is a direct adaptation of an earlier method, originally designed for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, and is adaptable to various well-posedness problems.

Kramer's theorem is widely recognized for its role in ensuring the degeneracy of magnetic materials. However, when these materials interact with their surroundings, Kramers degeneracy can be broken by certain types of external influences. This article explores a basic model that demonstrates such a breach, induced by a particular type of external driving force. It then goes on to propose a method of restoring the degeneracy through an internal type of quantum fluctuation. This approach is tested using a simplified model of a magnetic particle in an environment with random movements.

In highly mobile environments, accurately predicting channel state information (CSI) responses is crucial for optimizing wireless communication systems. To address this challenge, we propose a novel deep learning approach that leverages past CSI responses to forecast future ones. Our model incorporates a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, coupled with a convolutional neural network (CNN), to analyze spatial and temporal dependencies in CSI responses and generate forecasts based on these patterns. By doing so, we can mitigate the impact of sudden changes in mobile user movements on CSI feedback transmission.

A novel kernel density estimator is introduced to quantify the relationship between regression kernels, leveraging a parametric mixture model consisting of beta distributions with varying parameters. By employing an EM algorithm to determine the parameters, the method is applied to estimate minor regions in disparity measures and demonstrated using both simulated and real-world data sets, showcasing its capacity to accurately perform regression measure estimation.

This study establishes asymptotic formulas for the Szegö function on complex manifolds, specifically on real-analytic hypersurfaces embedded within complex spaces of higher dimensions. These asymptotic formulas are expressed in terms of the principal coexponential growth measure, a concept introduced in the paper. As a direct result, the study yields a large-dimension limit of the Bergman measure supported on real-analytic hypersurfaces within complex projective spaces of higher dimensions.

Redesigning an existing line chart to improve its readability can be achieved by rearranging data points, a process known as reverse line chart construction. Two methods for doing this are compared in this study. The first is a new, straightforward approach called MARINLINGA, and the second is a more complex method developed by Roussopoulos that maximizes the visibility of lines with the highest slope. A mathematical comparison between these two methods shows that MARINLINGA always produces a line chart with a superior alternative line of highest maximum slope. Furthermore, an algorithm implementing MARINLINGA's method requires only a single pass through the data, whereas Roussopoulos's method requires multiple passes. Their performance is compared through experiments using both synthetic and real-world data sets, with MARINLINGA's method found to outperform Roussopoulos's method.

To examine the hypothesis that the category of finitely presented projective modules over a domain has a dual topology to the hull topology of its full subcategory of torsion-free modules, we consider a specific domain with a particular property. We prove that this hypothesis holds true for a domain under two specific conditions: when it is a polynomial ring over a field with characteristic zero and when it is an elimination domain as defined by Vaserstein.

To maintain software system performance, it is essential to efficiently manage dependencies. Recent research focused on resolving dependency issues through refactoring, particularly in terms of renamed dependencies. This study examined the long-term effects of a common Java refactoring technique known as 'inflating' dependencies. By analyzing 6,000+ Java projects, it was found that inflating significantly increases dependency counts, with over 40% of projects experiencing a 100% increase and nearly 10% more than a 1000% increase. Although the frequency of renames and inflates decreased after the initial year, it is clear that developers require assistance in managing and organizing large repositories of dependencies.

In a recent experiment, we utilized a novel approach to entangled biphoton regulation in nanoscale synthesis. This method leverages a unique entangled state to control the growth of chains with varying monomer compositions. Our chosen approach utilizes an entangled biphoton source to regulate linearity and composition through the adjustment of branching ratio. This method has been successfully applied to the synthesis of polyethylene, which is a model system, to yield a dual-mode distribution. This resulting distribution is composed of two distinct peaks, each corresponding to different molecular weight and composition, as well as monodisperse and polydisperse polymers, respectively. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the composition of the polydisperse polymers adheres to a power-law distribution centered around the biphoton composition. This novel method has the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional methods, enabling the creation of complex, tailored structures.

This research focuses on solving complex multistage optimization problems that incorporate robustness against uncertain parameters in decision-making. A novel approach has been developed to create a subset of critical scenarios at each stage, referred to as an efficient scenario, which is defined by a distance metric. This method is tested using total variation discrepancy and evaluated in a specific case study, also known as the two-stage stochastic joint power generation and distribution planning problem. This method is further demonstrated with a case study that involves a utility company that owns a power plant and a distribution network, under uncertain load and power generation requirements. A numerical study has shown the method's efficiency and accuracy, also comparing it to other existing methods in the field.

Recent advancements in action prediction have led to the development of several innovative methods, which primarily focus on predicting the next action based on the current video frame or sequence. To address this task, researchers have employed recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks to model the dynamic and spatial aspects of actions, respectively. To enhance model robustness, data augmentation and feature normalization have been utilized. To improve predictive accuracy, methods such as ensemble learning and model selection have been applied. To mitigate overfitting, regularization techniques have been implemented. In this research, we introduce an RBF kernelized feature mapping RNN that utilizes a radial basis function kernel to enhance feature representation, which is then mapped to a higher-dimensional space to capture temporal dependencies. The resulting model exhibits superior performance on the UCF101 dataset, achieving a significant 10% improvement in accuracy over the current state-of-the-art method.

Deep neural networks are typically trained using a standard approach, known as backpropagation, which relies on gradient-based optimization. This method, however, can be limited in its ability to adapt to non-standard optimization requirements. This study focuses on an information-theoretic analysis of deep neural network training, specifically the process of minimizing a complex loss function in a high-dimensional parameter space. Our findings suggest that gradients alone may not always be sufficient to achieve this goal, unless the parameters are updated in a specific way, resulting in a unique form of thermalization. We also propose a solvable model that demonstrates these characteristics, which could have implications for understanding the effects of non-traditional update rules on neural network behavior.

We define a particular class of pseudo-differential operators on uniform trees and demonstrate their boundedness on the space of tempered distributions, relying on a methodical approach that incorporates combinatorial analysis. The main outcome can be interpreted as the property of being small in mass, which has an equivalent description in terms of the compactness of operators formed by the composition of pseudo-differential operators with specific re-embedding functions. The main theorem's validity extends to real coefficients; however, if the coefficients are complex, compactness cannot be inferred, and our analysis shows that the property of being small in mass is not necessarily hereditary.

The proliferation of mobile devices connected to the internet has led to the development of numerous mobile access networks, with 5G being the latest iteration. Smartphones, being the initial users of 5G and a key application, have driven the need for 5G network access. This study explores the presence of smartphones in 5G, highlighting their dominance over other devices within these networks. Data collected from a 5G test network in Europe, where users were intentionally introduced to utilize the network, demonstrate that smartphones are the most prevalent device type, accounting for more than 80% of all connections. This is true across all time periods, with minimal variation observed. This paper provides an in-depth examination of the data, revealing that devices connected to 5G networks exhibit distinct usage patterns compared to 4G networks.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) often display overconfidence when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) images. To address this issue, we've developed a new benchmark called Chamfer Out-of-Distribution Samples Against Overconfidence (CODEs) that includes 1,000 OOD images from 10 different classes per category, totaling 100 classes. To evaluate the performance of OOD detection models, we've designed a straightforward framework that uses the CODEs dataset. To validate the CODEs benchmark, we've created a range of baseline methods and tested them on this dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that the introduced methods can effectively detect OOD samples and minimize overconfidence.

The study of the $v_4$ and $v_2$ coefficients in the azimuthal distribution of jets in high-energy collisions has the potential to provide insights into the interactions within the quark-gluon plasma. In particular, it can reveal information about the formation of a color field and the energy loss of high-energy jets. To investigate these interactions, data from numerous events are required, which is why this study examines the $v_4$ and $v_2$ coefficients in large jet multiplicities. A novel method was used to analyze 2, 3, and 4-jet events from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, which included a large number of events. The results were compared to predictions from two different models, including Pythia 8 and Herwig 7, which showed that Pythia 8 performed better in predicting the $v_2$ coefficients but struggled with the $v_4$ coefficients. The study's findings have implications for heavy-ion collisions and the investigation of jet interactions within the quark-gluon plasma.

The increasing demand for semi-supervised learning and unsupervised learning has been driven by the escalating costs of annotating data and the desire to utilize large amounts of unlabeled data. Deep neural networks have been instrumental in recent breakthroughs in semi-supervised learning and unsupervised learning. This study provides a comprehensive review of the latest developments in semi-supervised learning and unsupervised learning based on deep neural networks. We examine the underlying principles of these approaches, evaluate the effectiveness of prominent semi-supervised learning and unsupervised learning models, and discuss the challenges associated with these methods. Furthermore, we discuss the applications of semi-supervised learning and unsupervised learning across multiple domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare. Finally, we highlight promising future research directions in this area.

Machine learning model performance is typically gaugged by standard evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F-score, yet these measures are inadequate for addressing the complex issue of anomaly detection. A major shortcoming lies in the reliance on predicted labels, which can be unreliable, especially when working with limited training data. Moreover, these metrics often prioritise accuracy on the normal class, overlooking the model's ability to identify anomalies. Consequently, the resulting evaluation metrics fail to accurately assess a model's ability to detect genuine anomalies. This paper presents RECol, a novel set of evaluation metrics that take into account the reconstruction error of both inliers and outliers, providing a more comprehensive assessment of the model's performance. The proposed metrics are based on the assumption that an inlier can be approximated by a normal distribution, while an outlier cannot. The proposed metrics are then compared to existing metrics using real-world datasets, with results indicating that RECol metrics effectively capture the model's ability to identify outliers, especially when compared to a baseline model.

We investigate solutions to a class of k-dimensional vector equations that involve a non-linear operator, specifically in a class of k+1-dimensional space, and establish a condition under which all solutions exhibit uniformity. This condition under which solutions have uniform growth rates is both necessary and sufficient. This class of equations encompasses many non-linear equations, including those with non-linearity in higher-order derivatives, that can be transformed into the more general form. Our findings have implications for random models, including those with non-Markovian characteristics, and provide insight into the behavior of certain stochastic processes.

Neutrino polarizability has significant implications for testing this concept, with recent findings from the MiniBooNE experiment indicating a value of $g_{e} = (2.15 \pm 0.28)\times 10^{-39}\,{\rm C}{\rm m}^2$ has drawn considerable attention. We have developed a novel approach to address the systematic uncertainties associated with the experiment's results, yielding a value of $g_{e} = (2.39 \pm 0.16)\times 10^{-39}\,{\rm C}{\rm m}^2$ that is nearly 50\% lower than the original finding.

Neuroscience research has long been searching for the mechanisms behind the rhythmic nature of brain activity.  A key aspect of this research involves understanding how the rhythmic activity of neurons is influenced by the surrounding neural tissue.  A recent study has shed new light on this issue by examining the effects of network connectivity on the rhythmic oscillations of neurons in a specific model system.  The model, which incorporates both neurons and glial cells, demonstrates how changes in the level of network connectivity can lead to the emergence of distinct oscillatory patterns, including both regular and irregular rhythms.  Notably, the model also reveals that increasing the level of network connectivity can lead to a shift from regular oscillations to more chaotic activity patterns.  These findings provide new insights into the role of network connectivity in regulating neural activity and highlight the importance of considering the complex interactions between neurons and their surrounding environment in understanding brain function and disease.

This study examines the topological characteristics of a neutral spin-1/2 particle's motion within an external magnetic field. We found that its behavior in the presence of multiple magnetic forces results in topological features such as Berry phases and Aharonov-Bohm effects at the quantum level, which are linked to non-Abelian and Abelian geometric structures respectively. We further investigated the impact of these forces on the particle's wave function and discovered that its dynamics is influenced by non-Abelian Berry connections. We further explored the connection between the particle's motion within different types of magnetic forces and found that its topological features are distinct, which is supported by the non-Abelian Bogoliubov transformation.

We introduce an innovative, time-efficient and energy-saving method for eroding a fixed obstacle within a flowing fluid in a confined space. This erosion process is driven by the fluid's movement after crossing a threshold at a specific entry point. No external forces or moving parts are involved. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that this 'initial-passage' method generates a unique type of boundary erosion featuring a 'fingerprint' pattern at early stages, and it eventually approaches but does not precisely replicate the self-organized gradient pattern observed in the traditional wave propagation erosion process. Our findings also reveal that the self-similar structure of the fluid flow around the obstacle dictates the long-term erosion pattern.

A hyperbolic link in $S^3$ with volume less than $5\pi/2$ is termed an L-space link if its corresponding hyperbolic manifold has an L-space geometry. We establish that for any L-space link, its associated pseudoholomorphic contact structure is equivalent to the standard contact structure on $S^3$. Furthermore, the semigroup generated by the lengths of the components of an L-space link, denoted as $L_1$, is proven to be characteristically equivalent to the semigroup of lengths of all classical L-space links. Consequently, this implies $L_1$ is a completely additive subset within the semigroup $\mathcal{K}_n$ of classical knots, and we derive a counterexample to show that $L_1$ does not necessarily satisfy the property of being a free semigroup.

We develop a Poisson mapping that links the microscopic, dissipative, inhomogeneous kinetic theory of gas mixtures to a hydrodynamic system with non-constant disorder terms. This mapping relies on the kinetic equation's collision operator, which must meet specific conditions to be compatible with the Poisson equation. Our work extends the previously established mapping for constant disorder terms to the kinetic theory with non-constant disorders, while ensuring the preservation of Hamiltonian properties through a suitable Lie transformation. The resulting hydrodynamic system is characterized by a non-conservative, inhomogeneous, and non-integrable dynamics. We demonstrate the existence of a suitable Poisson mapping with a disorder that changes over time and remains non-constant, which resolves the issue of determining the time evolution of disorder terms in kinetic theory.

Endoscopic procedures, a standard medical treatment, often involve the use of video recordings to monitor the procedure. However, these recordings frequently contain small objects that can signify anomalies, necessitating the assistance of specialized software to identify these objects accurately. To address this challenge, we propose a method for assessing the reliability of object detection models in endoscopic video, leveraging a collection of models to provide a confidence score for each detected object. Our approach is evaluated on a dataset of small objects, demonstrating that model reliability can be assessed through comparative performance between individual models and that model reliability in turn affects the overall accuracy of object identification.

In software engineering, understanding the syntax of programming languages is crucial, but the study of specific design patterns in code by combining different syntax elements has been largely overlooked. This research aims to address this gap by examining the emergence of different syntax patterns in code identifiers and their potential meaning in a specific context. A novel approach was developed to identify these patterns, which were then analyzed in the context of 1,894,671 code identifiers from open-source Java projects and 1,690,555 code identifiers from open-source C projects. The results show that certain common syntax patterns exist across different language frameworks and domains, but the specific meaning of these patterns varies between different projects and languages. This research demonstrates that syntax patterns have a meaningful connection to software design principles, suggesting that they could be used to inform or even automate the design process in future studies.

We introduce a novel infinite-dimensional $\square_q$-structure derived from the $q$-shuffle algebra K_q, which is associated with the affine Lie algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2$. This new structure is characterized by its product * on the direct sum of indecomposable modules over K_q, and involves a generalization of the q-binomial theorem. Furthermore, we establish that the *-algebra satisfies the Rota-Baxter identity with a specific weight-dependent operator. Building on this development, we explore the relationship between this new $\square_q$-structure and the affine quantum group U_q(wh), focusing on its connection to the affine quantum group's co-algebra.

The development of advanced materials for industrial applications, such as high-temperature alloys, metal matrix composites, and multi-phase alloys, has been identified as a key factor for next-generation materials. These multi-phase alloys can achieve exceptional strength and resistance to corrosion by combining the benefits of individual phases. However, predicting the growth of grains within these complex alloys remains a significant challenge. Our research utilizes a novel computational approach to investigate the kinetics of grain growth in various multi-phase alloys by analyzing the impact of distinct phase combinations on grain movement and growth. We have developed a statistical model that allows us to quantify the effect of grain movement and growth on the kinetics of grain growth in multi-phase alloys. Our findings, based on a comprehensive dataset of 1,200 simulations, reveal that grain growth kinetics in multi-phase alloys are primarily influenced by grain movement, grain-grain interactions, and the arrangement of phases. Our statistical model provides a straightforward and efficient way to predict grain growth kinetics in multi-phase alloys, enabling the development of predictive tools for designing future multi-phase alloys.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant progress in estimating human poses and shapes from a single RGB image. However, the evaluation of these models is often based solely on their performance, neglecting potential biases and limitations. This study proposes a systematic approach to assess and identify the strengths and weaknesses of existing human pose and shape estimation techniques. By considering various factors such as the human body, camera angles, and pose categories, the researchers aim to provide a more comprehensive understanding of these models. Through extensive testing, the study reveals that current techniques struggle with specific scenarios, including varying camera angles, pose categories, and body sizes. Building on these findings, the researchers introduce a new dataset, Human36mm-occlusion, which features images with missing individuals, as well as a modified version of Human3.6M with additional body parts for shape estimation. This new dataset is designed to facilitate further research in human pose and shape estimation.

The possibility of forming a superconducting phase in a system with significant electron-electron interaction is considered. In the context of the Hubbard model, this becomes feasible when the electron density on individual sites is low enough to prevent Mott insulating behavior. The resulting system of multiple interacting sites enables a superconducting state to emerge, with its strength contingent on the interplay of local repulsion and inter-site attraction.

This paper presents a systematic method for accurately matching scalar leptoquark interactions, focusing on two specific scenarios: one where leptoquark masses are relatively low and another where leptoquark masses are high but finite. By applying the leading logarithmic approximation, the method integrates out heavy degrees of freedom at the loop level and achieves precise matching at two-loop level. We detail the complete RGEs for each scenario and offer a corresponding Lagrangian in the MFV limit. Moreover, we demonstrate how to extend our results to the charged scalar leptoquark by incorporating additional CP-violating phases.

We demonstrate how employing classification theory can enhance both the understanding and validation of machine learning models, particularly neural networks, by providing a comprehensive overview of their capabilities and limitations. Our research findings are illustrated through the application to the ResNet18 model in the CIFAR-10 dataset.

A widely applied control method, terminal sliding-mode (TSM) control, is often used to achieve robust control in the presence of bounded uncertainties and disturbances. However, TSM controllers designed for second-order dynamic systems may not always result in asymptotic stability even when the control problem is well-defined. This issue arises due to the discontinuous nature of the sliding surface in TSM control and requires additional control law tuning. This study proposes a novel TSM controller with an ideal discontinuous sliding mode, specifically designed for second-order dynamic systems. The proposed design is supported by Lyapunov stability theory and is demonstrated through a practical example.

The performance of lithium-ion (LI-ion) batteries is significantly affected by the arrangement of their Li-active particles within their electrode structures. To address this, researchers have developed a novel electrochemical characterization technique that employs ultrasonic vibrations to precisely control the movement of lithium ions. By testing a commercial lithium-ion battery under different conditions, they discovered that the open-circuit resistance is largely influenced by the Li-ion particles' mean speed, while the resistance during the discharge phase is mainly affected by the voltage at which the discharge occurs. Based on these findings, the researchers developed a mathematical model that explains how the Li-ion particles' movement is restricted by the electrode structure. This model, along with their experimental data, allows for the quantification of the Li-ion particles' mean speed and the electrode structure's resistance. By applying this approach, the researchers were able to demonstrate that their technique can be used to assess the electrode structure of different cells and detect internal stress within the electrodes.

This research focuses on developing and testing a novel control method for a gantry crane, a complex, underactuated, continuous system with critical challenges. By applying the concept of discrete-time flatness-based tracking, the strategy overcomes the limitations of dealing with continuous-time systems and their non-linearities. Specifically, the approach involves transforming the tracking problem into a time-discrete format, where a specific, high-precision position trajectory is first created and then executed in real-time. Importantly, the proposed solution does not require the use of numerical approximators, and its efficacy will be demonstrated using a comprehensive case study involving a real-world gantry crane system.

The process of image captioning using data-driven learning has been successfully implemented in various applications. Nevertheless, there's a significant challenge in training these models with high-quality labeled data, particularly due to the scarcity of such datasets. Consequently, researchers have turned to alternative data sources, such as crowd-sourced online examples, to supplement these datasets, despite the inherent noise present in these alternative data sources. This study proposes an innovative approach called Co-Dist, which incorporates a cooperative learning strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy data in these alternative data sources. Co-Dist combines two distinct training objectives, including a standard beam search-based ranking loss and a novel consistency loss that measures the alignment between model predictions and ground-truth captions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Co-Dist in enhancing the performance of image captioning models trained on noisy data, particularly on the MSCOCO dataset.

characterizing finite sets of binary sequences that meet this new criterion of 
high connectivity. The main finding in this study is a direct extension of 
Hajnal's theorem, which initially characterized highly connected sets with a

This study introduces the concepts of a prearranged Ehresmann semigroup and prearranged Ehresmann category, both of which provide structured representations of a category with a locally associative and unital underlying structure. Key findings demonstrate that a prearranged Ehresmann category corresponds to a prearranged Ehresmann semigroup. Additionally, we establish a method for transforming a prearranged Ehresmann category into an Ehresmann category, thereby showing that a prearranged Ehresmann semigroup can be mapped to an Ehresmann semigroup under a given condition. The paper also explores the relationship between prearranged Ehresmann semigroups and monoids, as well as their connection to category theory.

Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of multi-layer perceptron (MLP) based self-attention mechanisms in tackling complex tasks, yet the dynamic relationship between depth and width remains poorly understood. This study investigates the depth-to-width interaction in self-attention, revealing that increasing both depth and width can lead to improved generalization, but may not always result in better test performance. We establish the optimal depth-to-width ratio for various tasks and observe that over-optimizing the width can compromise test performance while enhancing generalization. Furthermore, the optimal width depends on the target generalization performance, and over-optimizing the depth can yield significant improvements in test performance, particularly when the depth is insufficient.

A cost-effective method of synthesizing BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles through a reduction reaction in a solvent at 180-220 $\text{°C}$ is proposed. This novel approach yields high-quality nanoparticles with a particle size of 60-100 nm and reduced temperature processing, resulting in superior magnetic and photocatalytic properties. The reduced temperature synthesis enables the growth of specific crystal facets, enhancing the magnetization of the sample. The nanoparticles exhibit excellent photocatalytic activity for dye degradation and hydrogen production, outperforming those synthesized at higher temperatures. The results indicate that the novel synthesis method can be used to control the magnetization and photocatalytic activity of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles.

Within the framework of an extended Standard Model incorporating an exact $U(1)$ flavor symmetry, the masses of $b$ and $\tau$ quarks are expressed as definite fractions of the mass of the top quark. This particular flavor symmetry, however, fails to be preserved at higher orders of the perturbation theory. A thorough analysis of the symmetry-breaking patterns is carried out, followed by a discussion of the associated flavor-violating effects on quark and lepton masses.

Our goal is to accurately recreate the shape of an object in a hand, based on a single image, by combining 3D reconstruction with hand-object segmentation. To achieve this, we propose a new technique that can adapt to any object, without needing to learn its properties or the object's shape in advance. This is made possible through a two-stage process, where we first segment the image into the hand, the object, and the background, and then use this information to create a mesh of the object. To improve the accuracy of the hand and object segmentation, we use a novel method that incorporates spatial and contextual information, and we also leverage a large dataset of hand-object images to refine our model. Our approach significantly outperforms previous methods in hand and object segmentation and 3D reconstruction, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a variety of challenging real-world images.

The Ca-K index, an indicator of chromospheric activity in Sun-like stars, has been utilized for over five decades in solar research. This index serves as a direct measure of the number of active regions and can predict the solar irradiance variations. However, the method of calculating the Ca-K index has undergone significant changes since its inception. In order to accurately compare long-term Ca-K index data and apply the modern definition to historical data, it is essential to understand the modifications made to this index over time. In this study, we have identified and quantified the changes to the Ca-K index and its characteristics at the Kodaikanal Observatory using over a century of equal-contrast images. We have also created a database of the Ca-K index values at the Kodaikanal Observatory, spanning from 1908 to 2016.

The $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay is a rare occurrence that has garnered attention in the Standard Model effective field theory, particularly in the $NP\mu$ Wilson coefficient. A recent study involving the LHCb experiment has provided insight into this process, leveraging $2.0\,{\rm nb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at a 7 TeV centre-of-mass energy. By searching for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ in $\Lambda$ decays, researchers have established an upper limit on the branching fraction for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, yielding a value of $< 1.6$ times the Standard Model prediction at the 90% confidence level.

In the context of distributed software systems, a new approach for symbolic assessment is proposed, which utilizes a segmentation technique based on test-depth analysis to enhance efficiency. By leveraging this method, the assessment process is broken down into more manageable, prioritized segments, allowing for a more targeted evaluation of each domain component. This segmentation-based approach is then integrated with a collaborative assessment technique to optimize the assessment process. Furthermore, the approach is flexible and adaptable to varying domain structures and the analysis of external, system-wide inputs. We validate the effectiveness of this method through a case study of a distributed assessment tool, SmartWeb.

The rejuvenation process in arranged assemblies of magnetic nanoparticles is studied through simulations of the Monte Carlo method. These assemblies, comprising particles with varying sizes, are modeled as regular arrays of spheres, where smaller particles are embedded within layers of larger particles. The researchers utilize a three-spin model to capture the interactions between the smaller particles and the surrounding core-shell particles. The simulations demonstrate that smaller particles undergo rejuvenation as a result of their constrained movement within the core-shell layers, while the overall magnetic properties of the nanoparticle assemblies remain intact.

Federated learning effectively addresses data privacy concerns in distributed training by maintaining data confidentiality. However, its efficiency is compromised when data heterogeneity leads to slow model convergence. A novel approach, Central Hub Free Federated Training, overcomes this limitation, allowing for faster model training on large datasets with diverse data. By leveraging inter-user communication through the central hub, CHFFT promotes model convergence, particularly when paired with a proposed Free Federated Training optimizer that draws from the central hub and leverages machine learning as a service. A thorough evaluation of CHFFT and FFT optimizers demonstrates their effectiveness on real-world datasets.

In many real-world applications, the input to a short-text classification system consists of a sequence of texts, which must be combined into a unified representation before being fed into a neural network classifier. We propose and evaluate several neural architectures that incorporate recurrent and convolutional networks for short-text categorization, allowing each network to dynamically capture the significance of individual texts in the sequence. We also assess the impact of several loss functions on the system's performance, ultimately identifying the most effective approach. Our system achieved exceptional results in two real-world tests: a sequential news headlines categorization task and a user complaint analysis task at an Indian e-commerce company.

The telecentric Fabry-Pérot etalon is a versatile optical component that enables precise control over the phase and amplitude of light waves across broad frequency ranges. This study presents a comprehensive analytical framework for describing the optical response of telecentric etalons, encompassing resonant and non-resonant light, including or excluding the effects of diffraction. To achieve this, the etalon is divided into infinitesimely thin, perfectly reflecting sections, and the optical phase shift is derived through integration over these sections. This formulation is applied to investigate the optical response of resonant and non-resonant light, as well as to determine the optical constants of materials. Furthermore, the proposed method facilitates the derivation of a simplified etalon model, applicable to a broad range of optical configurations.

This paper proposes a novel technique, called suitable pairings, to identify and extract meaningful correlations from massive datasets. Suitable pairings are unique collections of data elements that share a common property, characterized by the frequency of their co-occurrence. The proposed method involves three key steps: identifying candidate pairings through data analysis, filtering out irrelevant pairings using a set of predefined rules, and validating the remaining pairings using an unsupervised clustering approach. The technique is demonstrated to be effective in discovering suitable pairings in both real-world and simulated data, highlighting its potential applications in network analysis and network-based classification tasks.

The development of the 5G wireless network has sparked significant interest in the field of Chiplets, which involve breaking down a system into smaller components of integrated circuits and combining them with interconnect solutions to enhance scalability and flexibility. This approach can lead to cost-effective design and on-demand production of customized baseband and RF processing systems. However, the integration of these components poses new challenges, particularly in terms of software development, testing, and verification. To address this issue, we propose the Codelet framework, which enables the development of compact, platform-independent software components for these components. This framework allows for the creation of software interfaces for these components and facilitates the development of software interfaces for these components and platforms. This is achieved through the use of microservices, REST-based interfaces, and JSON data formats. We also outline the development of a data model for these components and their interfaces, which can be used to define the structure and relationships between data elements. This data model can be represented in XML or JSON formats.

A novel approach to parameter estimation in finite-mixture models with a zero-inflated distribution is proposed, applicable to models where the recovery probabilities can be specified flexibly. This approach sidesteps the traditional maximum-likelihood estimation method when the number of components is greater than event times, overcoming computational difficulties. The approach instead estimates the recovery probabilities using a smoothing method, enabling consistent and asymptotically normal parameter estimators for both the cure distribution and mixture proportions. The method facilitates consistent estimation even when the number of components grows with sample size. The proposed estimator's asymptotic normality is demonstrated through Monte Carlo simulations, which validate its efficacy in finite-sample settings, including models with four or more components.

A graph's nonlocal distance dimension is defined as the smallest integer $d$ such that for any two distinct sets of vertices A and B with minimal distance greater than 2, there exists a set C satisfying the condition that all vertices in B are connected to a vertex in C and the vertices in A are located at a distance greater than d from the vertices in C from the graph's perspective.

In-memory computing technology, which enables rapid execution of complex tasks by utilizing data stored in the computing platform, has garnered significant attention for its exceptional performance capabilities. Nevertheless, the security features of in-memory computing systems have not received adequate consideration. This study undertakes a comprehensive security assessment of the oneTux framework, a leading in-memory computing framework for Linux, to identify potential security vulnerabilities. Our investigation, which involved a thorough examination of the oneTux stack, revealed that the lack of protection mechanisms in the framework against timing attacks and emulation-based attacks makes it vulnerable to side-channel assaults. Our testing results demonstrate that the oneTux framework is susceptible to side-channel attacks, which can compromise system security, yielding impressive attack success rates of up to 100% and remarkably high prediction accuracy of up to 99.79%.

We introduce reduced polarization kernels that enable the construction of polarization maps in active galactic nuclei (AGN) images by combining low-resolution data with a polarization information map. This approach offers an alternative to the generalized polarization derivatives used in the SHARP method, allowing for a direct reconstruction of mid-infrared polarization kernels. By applying the reduced polarization kernel method to simulated and real observations of the galaxy Mrk 766 with the SPICA/SPICA-RIPE, and utilizing the reduced polarization kernels from the mid-infrared and visible regions, we demonstrate comparable results to the SHARP mid-infrared kernel. Furthermore, we explore the potential of the reduced polarization kernels for future observations of AGN with the mid-infrared and visible regions, and highlight the advantages of the reduced polarization kernels over generalized polarization derivatives, including their ability to be computed analytically, yielding a more accurate polarization map, and facilitating the integration of multiple polarization maps with different resolutions and types.

A new method for noise reduction in seismic data has been proposed, which uses a self-supervised encoder-decoder model and a novel transfer learning approach in a transfer learning framework. The transfer learning framework utilizes an existing encoder-decoder model, which was previously trained on a synthetic dataset, to reduce noise in real seismic data. The transfer learning approach involves fine-tuning the model's weights to adapt to real seismic data through a recursive process of encoding, decoding, and fine-tuning. Additionally, this approach incorporates a regularization technique to prevent overfitting and improve the model's generalization. The proposed method was tested on a dataset of 12 seismic channels from a nearby source, and the results were compared with those obtained using existing machine learning-based and conventional noise reduction techniques. The results show that the proposed method outperforms others in terms of signal-to-noise ratio and peak ground acceleration accuracy.

The study of the electron-proton system through photon emission reveals a charge asymmetry, which is directly related to the inherent asymmetry in Z and $\bar{Z}$ photon form factors. This charge asymmetry is also present in positron-proton interactions, and it's a crucial factor in the difference between elastic lepton-proton and antilepton-proton scattering cross-sections. The inclusion of charge asymmetry in the description of the scattering process significantly affects the distribution of the real and virtual photon exchange in the process, and it's particularly notable at low Q^2 values.

We have conducted a theoretical study on the electronic properties of a 2D $d^5$ Mott insulator, specifically Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, using a combination of spin-orbit coupling and inter-octahedron interaction within a five-band Hubbard Hamiltonian. This model was solved using the Gutzwiller approximation and the results were compared with experimental scanning tunneling spectroscopy data. Our findings show that incorporating the inter-octahedron interaction yields a more accurate description of the observed spectrum, particularly at certain points. Furthermore, we found that accounting for this interaction is crucial in understanding the electronic behavior of this system, as neglecting it would only account for a fraction of the observed spectrum, specifically 40%, while the remaining portion can be attributed to inter-octahedron interaction.

Researchers are becoming increasingly interested in using machine learning techniques to assess causal mediation not only because of the wealth of available data but also because of the inherent interpretability of mediation analysis. Despite this interest, numerous challenges arise in mediation assessment, particularly in scenarios involving continuous treatments and outcomes. A major obstacle is the difficulty in establishing a concept of a mediator with a treatment effect when using a regression approach. This paper presents a novel method, referred to as "sturdy," for approximating mediation analysis in the context of continuous treatments and outcomes. Our proposed method employs a type of ensemble learning that mitigates the problem of model instability associated with single mediation models. Our simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances the accuracy of sturdy mediation assessment. Furthermore, we apply our method in a real-world study to examine the effect of the number of hours worked by medical trainees on their ability to diagnose patients and identify the role that work experience plays in this ability.

This editorial piece serves as an introductory gateway to a special publication of the SPIE Annual Meeting in San Diego, which showcased a diverse range of starshade proposals and design methodologies. The piece delves into the starshade concept and its potential to enhance exoplanet imaging capabilities. It also highlights the benefits of utilizing starshades in space-based missions, notes their development challenges, and outlines the progress made in both laboratory and field applications of starshades. Furthermore, the piece outlines the objectives and motivations behind the unique issue, which includes discussions on starshades, coronagraphy, and other related technologies that facilitate the detection of celestial objects.

The prevalence of mental health issues, including suicidal ideation, has been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the need for effective prevention and early intervention strategies. To address this challenge, advanced natural language processing techniques can be utilized to identify at-risk individuals and provide them with timely support. Developing reliable models for detecting suicidal risk relies on the creation of a comprehensive, annotated dataset that comprehensively captures the complexities of suicidal language. Unfortunately, existing datasets are limited in scope and scale. To address this limitation, our team has curated Robin, an extensive online collection of over 1.4 million posts from 201 an anonymous forum dedicated to mental health discussions. Robin offers unparalleled access to a diverse range of suicidal text, offering a valuable resource for researchers seeking to develop more effective detection models. To facilitate research, our dataset is publicly available, and we provide an in-depth analysis of its key features and the challenges of working with it.

A foundational concept in gravity research is the Schwarzschild metric, which has inspired numerous studies, particularly those focusing on the effects of gravitational fields on the motion of light. These investigations have been extensively explored and are often used as a basis for developing new gravitational theories. In contrast, this work introduces a novel approach, building upon the Schwarzschild solution, which instead yields a blackbody effect, thus dubbed "Blackian behavior." This idea is based on the idea of combining the Schwarzschild metric with a Planckian distribution, which is a more fundamental form of thermodynamics. As a result, this work demonstrates how a new metric emerges, which is a more general form of the Schwarzschild solution, which is a special case. In fact, this work shows that the new metric reduces to one that describes a blackbody at absolute zero, which is a more fundamental form of gravity than the Schwarzschild metric. The article focuses on examining the long-term behavior of solutions to a nonlinear difference equation, specifically $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants and $1<\alpha \leq2$. We derive general solutions to this equation and investigate the stability conditions for its bounded and periodic solutions. Our research demonstrates that the equation's behavior is heavily dependent on the values of $\alpha$, $a$, and $b$. Notably, we show that the difference equation can model population growth under certain conditions and that the resulting solutions accurately reflect real-world population data.

A novel approach to understanding the interaction of electric and gravitational forces in a 4-dimensional, spherically symmetric spacetime has been developed, based on a series of models that incorporate Born-Infeld's theory of electricity and general relativity. These models, which take into account the influence of an electric field, a cosmological constant, and a scalar field, were found to produce new types of black holes with distinct properties. Specifically, the models were found to have asymptotically AdS Schwarzschild-CFT black holes with varying degrees of deviation from the standard solution, and the influence of these deviations on the thermodynamic properties of the black holes was examined. Additionally, the models were found to have non-asymptotically AdS black holes with unique, non-linear electrodynamics characteristics.

A subset $\mathcal{A}$ of $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ is called $k$-Sidon if any $k$ distinct linear combinations of its elements result in distinct vectors. A collection of $L_{k}^{m}$ linear expressions over $k$ variables is called $k$-Sidon if the set of its evaluations when applied to $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ elements results in a $k$-Sidon subset. This study demonstrates that the number of possible $k$-Sidon collections of $n$ linear expressions over $k$ variables is at most $c_{k}p^{n}$. It also shows that this upper bound is tight, and more generally, the number of possible $k$-Sidon collections of $L_{k}^{m}$ linear expressions is at most $c_{k}(p^{m}/m)^{k}$. This is a key result in a broader study on Sidon sets, which also includes estimates for the number of possible Sidon subsets of $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ elements.

In the XY model, we investigate the behavior of magnetic susceptibility at finite temperatures, uncovering a phase transition from spatially uniform responses above the critical temperature, occurring at the critical temperature itself. Below the critical temperature, the form of magnetic susceptibility's temperature dependence undergoes a change and its spatial pattern, initially uniform at the critical temperature, splits into various modes at lower temperatures. This change occurs due to the emergence of Goldstone modes as the system transitions below the critical temperature, and our findings are supported by Monte Carlo simulations.

The concept of Kramers' theorem suggests that in an Ising model ferromagnet, a system with an even number of spin up particles experiences longer relaxation times than one with an odd number. This idea has been disputed by theoretical calculations indicating that Kramers theorem may actually lead to shorter relaxation times for even spin systems. To test this hypothesis, we conducted simulations of an Ising model on a two-dimensional lattice at different temperatures, and found that the hypothesis was proven false.

We examine the behavior of two-dimensional quasicrystals with long-range hopping, where the hopping strength decreases as a low-power function of distance. Using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we discover that when the quasicrystal is represented by a 10x10 matrix, localized states can emerge at low energies, even when the quasicrystal is connected. Notably, these localized states can coexist with extended states at the Fermi energy. The characteristics of these localized states depend on the specific power function used, localized states can either be highly correlated or uncorrelated, depending on whether the quasicrystal is connected or not, respectively.

Emerging multilingual conversational systems are being developed to cater to diverse populations, leveraging natural language understanding capabilities to comprehend input queries. Although significant progress has been made in NLP, particularly with the advent of pre-trained language models, creating effective multilingual dialogue systems is a complex task requiring specialized expertise in natural language processing. This work aims to bridge the knowledge gap by providing a foundational guide, highlighting recent advancements in NLP that facilitate task-focused dialogue system development. We focus on three task-oriented applications: question answering, definition explanation, and fact verification, and illustrate how established NLP techniques, such as query reformulation and answer prediction, can be adapted to build efficient conversational response systems.

Alternative splicing is a process that significantly impacts the human genome's transcriptome. It's a crucial process that's home to approximately half of all alternative transcripts, which are typically expressed at low levels. To better understand alternative splicing, we've developed a statistical model that can quantify the impact of various regulatory factors on the process. Our model, which relies on RNA-seq data, can predict the relative expression of alternative transcripts, as well as their corresponding mRNAs. We've also used our model to show that alternative splicing is a dynamic process that's heavily influenced by a variety of factors, including the type of alternative splicing event and the developmental stage of the cell. We've also found that alternative splicing is often associated with changes in gene expression, and that it's typically regulated at the level of alternative splicing rather than transcription.

Developers working on data-intensive projects often encounter a complex interplay between privacy and performance.  In response, they employ technical strategies to meet privacy requirements while optimizing performance, yet little research has explored the methods used to execute these strategies or the impact on developers' comprehension. This research investigates how professionals implement technical measures to ensure data privacy and understand the underlying relationship between these strategies and developers' knowledge. A qualitative study was conducted with 38 experts through surveys and in-depth interviews, revealing a diverse range of measures used to ensure data privacy and revealing critical knowledge gaps. The study also identified key factors contributing to developers' difficulties in understanding these strategies, including the necessity of specialized knowledge, the blurring of lines between technical roles, and the lack of relevant documentation. The study's findings have implications for teaching data privacy principles, designing software engineering courses, and developing tools that facilitate the execution of these strategies.

The initial state of nuclear collisions can be examined through multi-particle correlations in the final state. Specifically, we analyze directional azimuthal correlations involving at least one hadron in peripheral proton-lead collisions at the LHC. Using a simplified model, we demonstrate how to calculate directional azimuthal correlations involving at least one charged hadron in the binary process of proton-lead collisions. Applying the HYDJET++ model, we study the characteristics of directional azimuthal correlations, including the two-particle correlations and three-particle correlations with a leading hadron. Additionally, we investigate the effects of varying the lead nucleus's impact parameter and the presence of a color glass condensate, as well as the potential of these correlations to reveal the nucleus's transverse profile.

The creation of light nuclei in heavy collision systems is studied through a comprehensive model that incorporates hadron resonance production and statistical freeze-out. This model explains how the yields of various light nuclei are produced via different coalescence origins, including the formation of baryon clusters, hadron clusters, and hadron resonances. We examine how the collision energy influences the coalescence origins and present predictions for the production of light nuclei in Au-Au collisions at 3 GeV. Future research aims to experimentally verify these findings through an upcoming experiment at the BNL STAR collaboration.

The discovery of hundreds of exoplanets has led to a significant shift in
exoplanet research, from studying the atmospheric properties of single,
isolated planets to understanding their environments and the complex systems
they form and influence. As we explore the vast multitudes of exoplanets, we
now recognize the importance of considering their surroundings and the planetary
atmospheres' interactions. The accumulation of data from ongoing and future
missions has enabled us to examine various aspects of exoplanetary environments
and their effects on planetary atmospheres. In this review, we focus on the
interactions between atmospheric loss and radiation, the impact of stellar
variability, the effects of magnetic fields, and the interactions with nearby
planets and their rings. We also explore the role of environments in shaping
life and the possibilities of studying exoplanetary environments through the
upcoming James Webb Space Telescope observations.

The existence of a regular graph G implies the existence of a set S with low cardinality that can label the vertices of G uniquely. A minimal set with this property for a specific graph G is called G's minimal solubility set and the cardinality of this set is called G's solubility number. Historically, determining the solubility number for any given graph has been a difficult problem, but for certain types of circulant graphs, this question was partially answered decades ago with a key limitation - the set in question must contain all prime numbers up to a specific, prime number p such that p^2 is divisible by the number of vertices in the circulant. In this paper, we resolve this previously unsolved problem by demonstrating that any circulant with a number of vertices, n, that can be divided evenly by n/2 and contains a specific, prime number p such that p^2 is divisible by n can be labelled using a set containing all prime numbers up to p, thus establishing the solubility number as p.

This paper presents an enhanced approach to the Elevated Power Method, utilizing it to accelerate iterative matrix inversion techniques and examining the effects of varying the power parameter on convergence speed. We also derive improved error bounds for the Elevated Power Method and show that using an optimal power value can achieve superior convergence performance over other related iterative methods. To facilitate GPU implementation, we introduce two new power-based techniques - Elevated High Power Exponentiation with Hyperpower and Elevated Power Exponentiation - outperforming the existing Elevated Power Method. We demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methods, High Power Exponentiation with Hyperpower and Elevated Power Exponentiation, in comparison to state-of-the-art iterative methods such as the Hessenberg-Liu, symmetric Hessenberg, and symmetric Jacobi methods. Moreover, we show that our approaches achieve faster convergence rates than the High Power Exponentiation with Hyperpower technique.
